# SpatialDiscreteChoice

## `BayesianSpatialProbitModel`

    BayesianSpatialProbitModel

A spatial probit estimated by Albert-Chib Gibbs sampling, returned by
[`fit_bayesian_spatial_probit`](@ref).

Data augmentation draws the latent utilities, which makes the conditional
posteriors tractable and avoids the intractable likelihood. Slower than
[`fit_spatial_probit`](@ref) but markedly more precise on `rho` in small
samples, and it carries an intercept.

This is built in, not part of the Turing extension.

## `SpatialOrderedProbitModel`

    SpatialOrderedProbitModel

A spatial ordered probit, returned by
[`fit_spatial_ordered_probit`](@ref), for an outcome with `J` ordered
categories.

Alongside the coefficients it carries the cut points separating the
categories, drawn from their uniform conditionals between adjacent order
statistics of the latent vector.

With `J = 2` this reduces to binary probit, which
[`fit_bayesian_spatial_probit`](@ref) handles better since it carries an
intercept.

## `SpatialProbitEffects`

    SpatialProbitEffects

Direct, indirect and total marginal effects on the probability scale for a
spatial discrete-choice model, returned by [`marginal_effects`](@ref).

Two things compound here: the probit link makes the effect depend on where
each unit sits on the curve, and the spatial lag propagates a change
through `(I - rho*W)^{-1}`. The reported effects average over both.

## `SpatialProbitModel`

    SpatialProbitModel

A spatial probit fitted by linearized GMM, returned by
[`fit_spatial_probit`](@ref).

Fast, because it avoids the `N`-dimensional integral the exact likelihood
needs, but less precise in small samples than the Gibbs sampler — see
[`fit_bayesian_spatial_probit`](@ref) when precision on `rho` matters.

Use [`marginal_effects`](@ref) to interpret the fit: as in any probit the
coefficients are not marginal effects, and the spatial lag adds feedback on
top of that.

## `fit_bayesian_spatial_probit`

    fit_bayesian_spatial_probit(W, X, y; n_samples=2000, burnin=500, rng=...)

Fit the spatial autoregressive probit by Gibbs sampling with Albert & Chib
(1993) data augmentation, following LeSage & Pace (2009, Ch. 10).

Each sweep: draw the latent `y*` one site at a time from its truncated
conditional, draw `β` from its conjugate normal conditional, then update `ρ` by
random-walk Metropolis on `log|I-ρW| - ½(Ay*-Xβ)'(Ay*-Xβ)` with a Uniform(-1,1)
prior. The error variance is fixed at 1 for identification.

`beta_prior_var` sets an isotropic N(0, v·I) prior on β. Reported `coef` and
`vcov` are the posterior mean and covariance; `accept_rate` is the ρ acceptance
rate, which should land roughly in 0.2–0.5. The default `rho_proposal_sd` of 0.2
targets that band; 0.05 overshoots to about 0.77 acceptance and mixes slowly.

Because the observed signs pin the latent vector only up to scale, ‖β‖ and ρ
trade off along a weakly identified ridge, and at small `N` the posterior is
not centred on the truth. Over 40 replications on rook lattices at ρ = 0.4,
with the chain at its default length:

| N | ρ bias | β₁ bias | ρ coverage | β₁ coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 36 | −0.161 | +37.9% | 87.5% | 97.5% |
| 64 | −0.160 | +23.6% | 80.0% | 92.5% |
| 144 | −0.059 | +5.5% | 90.0% | 92.5% |
| 256 | −0.025 | +3.1% | 92.5% | 97.5% |

β₁ bias is a percentage of its true value. The Monte Carlo standard error on
the ρ biases is 0.045 at `N = 36` falling to 0.018 at `N = 256`, so the first
two are well clear of zero and the last is marginal. ρ is pulled toward zero
and ‖β‖ pushed out together — that pairing *is* the ridge — and both decay
with `N`.

This is a property of the posterior at small `N`, not a mixing failure, so a
longer chain does not remove it. At `N = 64`, over 30 replications on
identical data, going from 1500 draws to 20000 raised the effective sample
size for ρ from 75 to 929 while the ρ bias held at −0.107 and −0.101 and the
β₁ bias at +0.197 and +0.194. Lengthen the chain to cut the Monte Carlo error
in one chain's summaries — at the defaults the effective sample size for ρ is
only about 100, so `vcov` and the posterior mean carry a few percent of noise
— but read a small-`N` ρ as biased toward zero whatever the chain length.
Check `accept_rate` sits in 0.2–0.5. When `N` is small and ρ is the quantity of
interest, [`fit_spatial_probit`](@ref) is the better choice: its ρ bias runs
the other way and is smaller from `N = 64` up (+0.044 at 64, +0.008 at 144,
against −0.112 and −0.058 here on the same data).

!!! note "Identification"
    The design has to have full column rank. `X` goes in without an
    intercept, since one is added, and no covariate may be a linear
    combination of the others. A design that fails this throws an
    `ArgumentError` naming the offending column, rather than failing
    inside the linear algebra or returning an arbitrary split of one
    coefficient across two.

    The sampler is the case where this matters most: nothing factorises and
    fails, so a dependent column simply produces a posterior that splits one
    coefficient across two columns.

## `fit_spatial_ordered_probit`

    fit_spatial_ordered_probit(W, X, y; n_categories=maximum(y), n_samples=2000, ...)

Fit the spatial ordered probit

    y* = ρWy* + Xβ + ε,    y = j  iff  τ_{j-1} < y* ≤ τ_j

by Gibbs sampling with data augmentation (Wang, Kockelman & Wang, 2013).
`y` holds integer categories `1:J`.

For identification there is no intercept and `τ_1 = 0`; the free cutpoints
`τ_2 … τ_{J-1}` are drawn from their uniform conditionals between the adjacent
order statistics of the latent vector. `τ_0 = -∞` and `τ_J = +∞`.

A binary `y` (J = 2) reduces to the probit above and is better served by
[`fit_bayesian_spatial_probit`](@ref), which carries an intercept.

The weak identification described for the binary sampler applies here too,
and the free cutpoints move with it. Over 80 replications at `N = 64`, `J = 3`,
ρ = 0.35: ρ bias −0.031, β biases +0.096 and −0.068, coverage 93.8%, 95.0% and
91.2%. `τ_2` came out +0.103 high, the same proportional inflation as ‖β‖,
because cutpoints and coefficients share the latent scale. `τ_1` is exactly 0
in every draw by construction.

!!! note "Identification"
    The design has to have full column rank. `X` carries no intercept
    here — the cutpoints hold the level — so a constant column in `X` is
    itself the rank-deficient case, as is any covariate that is a linear
    combination of the others. Either throws an `ArgumentError` naming the
    column.

## `fit_spatial_probit`

    fit_spatial_probit(W, X, y; varnames=nothing, instrument_lags=2)

Fit the spatial autoregressive probit model

    y* = ρWy* + Xβ + ε,    y = 1(y* > 0)

by the linearized GMM estimator of Klier & McMillen (2008). A standard probit
supplies the ρ = 0 starting value; the moment conditions are then linearized
around it and estimated by 2SLS with instruments `[X, WX, W²X]`.

`y` must be coded 0/1. Returns a `SpatialProbitModel`.

Fitted probabilities use the heteroskedastic latent form
`Φ(((I-ρW)⁻¹Xβ)ᵢ / √[(I-ρW)⁻¹(I-ρW)⁻ᵀ]ᵢᵢ)`, which needs a dense inverse of
`I - ρW`; cost is O(N³), so this is intended for moderate N.

`loglikelihood` reports the probit log-likelihood evaluated at the fitted index.
It is a pseudo-likelihood — the estimator is GMM, not ML — so it is comparable
across specifications fit the same way, but is not an ML criterion.

Linearizing around ρ = 0 buys speed at a real cost in efficiency. Over 8
replications at ρ = 0.4 this estimator had a standard deviation of about 0.25 at
N = 196 and 0.18 at N = 400 — roughly 2.5× that of
[`fit_bayesian_spatial_probit`](@ref) on the same data. It is approximately
unbiased, so treat a single small-sample ρ̂ as a coarse reading and prefer the
Gibbs sampler when precision on ρ matters.

!!! note "Identification"
    The design has to have full column rank. `X` goes in without an
    intercept, since one is added, and no covariate may be a linear
    combination of the others. A design that fails this throws an
    `ArgumentError` naming the offending column, rather than failing
    inside the linear algebra or returning an arbitrary split of one
    coefficient across two.

## `marginal_effects`

    marginal_effects(m::SpatialProbitModel)

Decompose the marginal effect of each covariate into direct, indirect, and total
components. For covariate `k` the effect matrix is `diag(φ(index)) (I-ρW)⁻¹ βₖ`;
the direct effect averages its diagonal, the total averages its row sums, and
the indirect effect is the difference (LeSage & Pace, 2009).

Requires a dense inverse of `I - ρW` — O(N³), so intended for moderate N.
